utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said earlier that the Albanian newspaper Koha Ditore refused to publish an appeal from the Serbian government to Kosovar Albanians to remain and not to leave. When was this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sometime in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, was it before or after the conflict started, before the NATO bombing started?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before -- if you mean before the aggression, it was before the aggression, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that at the start of the aggression the printery of that newspaper was burned down and the MUP entered the premises and a guard was killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no; but to the best of my knowledge at the beginning of the NATO aggression the printing works were not burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to move on to ask you about some of the forces that were present in Kosovo at the time when you were security chief of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P1415, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while it is coming up, can I ask you some -- ask you whether or not you have heard or seen in Pristina Corps orders the term "armed non-Siptar population"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the orders of the Pristina Corps, I did see this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what, if any, was their role in operations or actions during the war after March 24, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer your question. In mid-1998 the situation in Kosovo and Metohija was exceptionally difficult. Many settlements inhabited by Serbs sent representatives to the corps command, who asked the corps commander that the army protect them or that they be issued with weapons so that they can protect themselves, in view of the fact that many small Serb enclaves had been burnt down and looted. I attended meetings held by General Pavkovic, the commander of the Pristina Corps at the time, when the villagers of the village Priluzje in Obilic municipality came to see him and asked him to distributed weapons to him. The corps commander forwarded all such requests to the Ministry of Defence because that was the competent organ able to issue such a decision. After June 1998, I am aware that following an order from the Pristina Corps commander to his subordinate units, they were ordered to arm their military conscripts in smaller ethnic communities where Serbs lived. I'm also aware that these conscripts remained in their villages to defend their villages, and I have no information that the inhabitants of those villages participated in any kind of combat against the terrorists outside their own villages. They were simply protecting and guarding their own villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you as -- or did you as chief of security of the Pristina Corps know how many such persons were armed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any precise information about that. I don't know, but there are records with the units that did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you tell us roughly how many this would amount to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe some 40.000 let's say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I don't think we need to go through the document which I just called up, which I think is in front of you. They were commanded by the VJ, were they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not commanded by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 of this document, P1415. It's page 2 in the English, I'm sorry, it's page -- still remains page 1 in the B/C/S. I should have indicated that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There you can see in the last three paragraphs or in the -- in paragraph 6 it indicates they are formed: "In each village according to the military structure in squads, platoons, and companies. Appoint a commander, deputy, and assistant for each unit. Organize the defence of settlements so that each settlement has sentries, patrols, ambushes, duty units, an intervention unit and an evacuation unit." And then the last paragraph in 6: "Place an active superior officer in charge of each settlement to directly control the preparation of units and remain there until the organization of defence is fully completed and the unit is trained." Didn't the VJ retain control over these armed units even after that period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, first let's comment on this document, which I see before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, answer and then comment.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document dates from June 1998 when the military territorial organs, through the command of the military district, were subordinated to the command of the 3rd Army and not the Pristina Corps. If you look at the document carefully it says that the military departments are responsible for organizing the defence of those villages. This means that they were to prepare and organize the population, to protect their own villages if attacked by terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but this is an order signed by the corps commander at the time, Major-General Pavkovic, and it provides that these villagers should be trained by the VJ and that the VJ should make plans for the maintenance and storage of the weapons that they were given. And you can see there that they were given assault rifles, sniper rifles, and weapons of this nature. Isn't it true, General, that the VJ did retain control of these village units in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, from this document which I see before me, I can say that the representatives of the subordinate units on whose territory there were villages inhabited by Serbs which were completely surrounded and under threat were duty-bound, according to the appropriate military occupational specialties, to arm men liable for military service in those villages and train them how to defend those villages through patrols, guards, sentry duty in their own villages. That's my interpretation of this document, but I don't know what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. The question is simple. This document speaks to the formation of these units in the middle of 1998 and it tells you that the VJ trained them, armed them, and was responsible to secure and maintain the arms, and these are combat arms, assault rifles and sniper rifles included. And the question is, having regard to all of that: Didn't the VJ retain control over these units in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these armed villages and the units in those villages which were armed, never left their own villages. I say that with full responsibility. Throughout the war they remained in their villages defending their villages from any terrorist attacks. If you're asking me whether they were used beyond the boundaries of their villages and their homes, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where they were used, whether in defence of their villages or outside the villages, wherever, the question is simple: Did the VJ retain control over these units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military territorial organs retained control, the ones that were competent, to make sure that the weapons were not abused, were not misused. I have to correct you. They did not have snipers; they had semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if we could look at page 1 in English, maybe I was mistaken there. And when we are looking at page 1 you will agree with me that the military territorial organs were under the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They were under the command of the Pristina Military District, and the command of the Pristina Military District was under the command of the 3rd Army, all the way until April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Thanks, sir. It might be a minor thing, but doesn't paragraph 2 indicate the weapons that were distributed to them. It says: "Distribute automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, light machine-guns, sniper rifles, necessary communications equipment," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir, I'll explain. That's what it says here, but I know that the Pristina Corps did not have enough sniper rifles for the military police or the special units, let alone to distribute to villagers, to inhabitants, of Serb villages in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. The part of the order that I read earlier at paragraph 6, it said that there were -- within these units they were to form an intervention unit. We have heard some evidence in the court about what intervention units were in the VJ, but can you tell us what an intervention unit was in these village units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Security for the villages threatened by terrorists, primarily non-Albanian villages, was organized as follows: Night guards were organized, check-points at entrances to the villages, and if a sentry post or a check-point was attacked there was a unit inside the village ready to intervene on the axis from which the village was being attacked. These were not intervention units which would leave the village and chase the enemy; they would simply close off certain axes to prevent the terrorists from entering the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you explain why it would be the Pristina Corps commander that was ordering his various commanders to carry out this exercise of arming these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably those were his orders from the superior command, the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would that be the case if the appropriate way of dealing with this is through the Pristina Military District?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't really answer that. Probably this was done in coordination with the command of the military district. This was in June 1998 when the military district was quite separate from the command of the Pristina Corps with reference to the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Precisely. So that's why I'm asking you, why should the Pristina Corps be involved? Can you help or do you just not know or as a security chief was it not something you were likely to know about or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you look at the preamble to this document, the first paragraph, it says: "Pursuant to orders from the command of the 3rd Army, strictly confidential order number," such and such, "and the aggravated political and security situation ..." He's ordering the commander of the Pristina Corps to order his subordinate commanders to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got all that, Mr. Stojanovic. My question is: Why would the Pristina Corps get such an order when the right way to deal with this is through the Pristina Military District, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably because the Pristina Corps had better officers among their personnel, more expert personnel, able to do this, because in the military territorial detachments, I don't know if you want me to tell you this, but these were just a few officers, just some officers who in peacetime sat in those offices in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware of this order at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you can't remember the circumstances? You can only speculate about why this might have been done. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Quite simply, physically -- well, I'll explain. On the territory of Prizren municipality there are four or five villages. Only five officers were working in the military department. So in physical terms and organizational terms, they would not have been able to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's taken a long while to get to that answer. Earlier you told me that you thought they probably had been ordered to do it in conjunction with the military district. It doesn't sound as though you really know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced I do know, Your Honour. It says here that the military departments are duty-bound only to organize once weapons had been issued, to organize the villagers for the defence of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could discuss briefly another topic. Many of the reports that you discussed when the counsel for Mr. Lazarevic was asking you questions, that is, reports from your sector, telegram that you sent, used or referred to the sources of information including the RDB, that is, the state security department. And I believe after the war or later on you did say in an interview that much of the information from this source that you relied upon during the war turned out to be wrong, turned out to be unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, when it refers to the situation on the state border with the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you -- are you aware also that General Dimitrijevic complained about the unreliability of some of the reports that was coming up to the security headquarters in Belgrade from the security section in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the chief, General Dimitrijevic never made any remarks about my reports; on the contrary, he was very satisfied with my reports. And there are many records from his visits, his tours, and my reports, and he was very satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we do have a couple documents, one of them being for the record P928, but I just represent to you now that we do have a couple documents of General Dimitrijevic at collegium meetings of the Chief of Staff of the VJ complained to General Ojdanic about the reliability of some of the reports that were coming up. Now never heard of that? You never heard of these complaints?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what period General Dimitrijevic's complaints refer to. I told you that in the course of the war I reported to the security department of the 3rd Army, and throughout 1998 also directly to General Dimitrijevic through telegrams, and there was not a single complaint. I repeat, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have some additional questions for you. We can first go back to the document shown to you just a minute ago, P1415. If we can -- yes, we see it on the screen. General, in this document, does this refer to military conscripts or men liable for military service?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Secondly, can we look at item 5 and can you tell me whether it also provides for the storage of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it describes in detail how the weapons are to be stored which are to be distributed to these conscripts and how they're to be kept under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And they are military conscripts who have their wartime deployment, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the end of the page, the end of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, could you interpret what it says in the last sentence there. It says that an active officer should be placed in charge who will be responsible for preparing the units and will stay until the entire defence is set up and the unit trained. Can you explain to us what that means "remain there until the organization of defence is fully completed and the unit trained"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said a moment ago. There was an active officer in charge for each post who was in charge of preparing the units, and it was his duty to remain until everything was set up, the whole organization of defence and until the unit had been trained to handle the weapons they had been issued, so the whole concept of the village's defence should the village come under terrorist attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But if it says "remain until the unit is trained," does he have any responsibility afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no authorisations afterwards, just until they are trained, and then he goes back to his own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'm now going to start off with the cross-examination that my learned colleague Mr. Stamp conducted with you on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we take a look at Exhibit P2297, please, and it is -- [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have lost interpretation I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English? Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we can now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let's take a look at the date, which is the 17th of April, 1999. And my question is this: First of all, the military police battalion, was it an independent battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. It was one of the independent battalions linked to the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The military police battalion, did it have it commander; and if so, what was the commander's name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like any other battalion, the 52nd Battalion of the military police had its commander and his name was Major Stevo Kopanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Part of that battalion and to what extent, was it on the 17th of April resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not part of it, no, not to the 125th Motorised Brigade because of the very serious situation along the border towards Albania in the area of responsibility of that brigade, and especially in the Kosare border post where the brigade lost 63 of its members who were killed by the terrorists which were carrying out an all-out offensive from the territory of Albania. It was reinforced, or rather, it was -- a military police company was resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, we have here the war diary or the war log on our screens. Now, under the 17th of April, can you find that piece of information in the entry there? Does it correspond to what you're testifying about now if we look at the entry for the 17th of April and it's under number 2, "our forces," the "cVP," is that the military police company which was attached to the 125th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and it was engaged in fighting against the terrorists in Rasa e Kosare which is around the Kosare border post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try to confine yourself to answering the questions and we'll make a lot more progress. We don't need the extra; if Mr. Bakrac wants it, he'll ask for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When the military police company was resubordinated to the 125th, who commanded it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether part of that company was replaced at any point in time during April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the company engaged in heavy fighting, and I think that around the 20th of April the deputy battalion commander visited the company and replaced part of the men that were -- and they were pulled out from the fighting in the Kosare border post area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That company, did it in part participate in the action Reka?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that two platoons from that company took part in the Reka action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, on Friday, His Honour Judge Chowhan asked you: Why didn't you go to Kosovo and Metohija to conduct an investigation. Now, within the frameworks of the set of questions asked to you by Mr. Stamp yesterday I would like to ask you some questions too. So tell me this, please: When did you leave Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Kosovo and Metohija on the 16th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia at the time and the MUP all left Kosovo completely?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The withdrawal of the army and MUP from Kosovo lasted from the 10th to the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After that did any state organ or anybody else, were they able to conduct any kind of investigation on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no state organ could enter Kosovo and Metohija at all, let alone conduct any investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And can they do that today, to this day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the civilian administration of the international community has been set up in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yesterday my learned friend Mr. Stamp asked you something about the indictment published at the end of May. Now, I would like to ask you this: Do you know against whom the indictment was raised in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against the former president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At the end of May or the beginning of June, apart from that piece of information, did you have any knowledge about the contents of that indictment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any information about the contents of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any information at that time that in the indictment there was a member of the Pristina Corps perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was not a single member of the Pristina Corps there in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The military prosecutor attached to the Pristina Corps command or the military district of Pristina, did you receive any assignment to gather information and data linked to that indictment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, not from any organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you receive instructions from the 3rd Army superior security officer to undertake an investigation of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no instructions at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you testified here and said that between the 1st of June and the 7th of June, 1999, there was a team from the security administration of the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, so that was after the indictment was published. Did they perhaps give you -- make some demands or give you instructions or did they comment on the indictment and give you certain tasks with respect to investigating anything?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team from the security administration who was in the Pristina Corps at the period of time you mentioned made no mention of the indictment at all, nor did they issue any tasks or give me any instructions with regard to the indictment or any security organ, and we toured them together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Stojanovic, that when you learned of the indictment you did not know it related to ethnic cleansing, you did not know that it made accusations of Serb forces committing murder? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I learned about the indictment through the information media, and as to the contents of the indictment it was many months later that I had an opportunity of getting to know the specific contents of that indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is simpler than that. Are you saying that the information media did not tell the public that this indictment related to allegations of ethnic cleansing in Kosovo, including murder, committed by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, the indictment referred to all the territories, or rather, the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, and Kosovo and Metohija, and in it, it said if -- for persecution, killing, the killing of Albanians, civilians, and some other details. So as I say, those are the contents that I knew about, but it was many months later that I learnt about that, far after it had been published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This may explain your confusion yesterday about dates because in May 2000 -- in May 1999 there was no indictment relating to Croatia or Bosnia. The only indictment that was issued at that time related to Kosovo. Now, think back and tell us again when it was you first became aware of the indictment against Milosevic and others relating to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already said when it was disclosed in the information media in my country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So now that we're clear on that, can you remember the date when it was disclosed or roughly how long after the indictment was issued it became public to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't say. I can't remember, and I don't want to hazard a guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when you first heard of it were you aware that it related to allegations of ethnic cleansing carried out by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean Kosovo, then yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were you aware also that the allegations included murder on a large scale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's against that background that you're being asked: Was this not something you felt ought not to be investigated, bearing in mind that apparently the publication was prior to the end of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, and I'll give you three reasons. The first is the following, and I said that yesterday: I am quite certain of the work of -- of my work and the police security organs with respect to documenting and prosecuting crimes committed by members of the army. The other reason, the second reason, is this. As of August I was outside the military security service, and I had no authority under the law to undertake any measures to investigate the crimes mentioned on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. And the third reason, as I've already stressed, no legal court organ issued instructions to me to undertake such measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, General, you've just said you didn't have the authority to do that. Now, as of June until August, while you were in the service, did you have authorisation to act upon the indictment against Milosevic without instructions from the prosecutor or the security administration?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And immediately after the war, after June, when you returned and when the authority was passed to the prosecution office of the court in Nis and up till August when you were in the security organ from the prosecutor, were you given any assignment in the sense of conducting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single act in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you know, or rather, you testified and told us that the security organ, the investigating judge, and a team for exhumation conducted an investigation on the -- in the Slovinje locality during the war in 1999. Now, do you know that the UNMIK police in Kosovo launched proceedings against certain civilians on the basis of the findings that, among other things, on the basis of the exhumation results conducted by the Army of Yugoslavia or its professional organs, the investigating judge, the security organ, and the pathologist?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of our criminal report, the one we filed, and our knowledge, the knowledge we gathered, I know that sometime in 2005 I believe, five individuals from the Lipljan area, which is where Slovinje is located, were taken into custody and were prosecuted for the crimes stipulated that took place in the locality and this was based on our data and information, and it was seen that they were not members of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, my learned friend Mr. Stamp asked you something about the corpses found in Batajnica. Now, do you have any knowledge and information to the effect that the Army of Yugoslavia took part anywhere in digging up the bodily remains in any area in Kosovo and Metohija and transporting them to Serbia? Do you have any knowledge of that, and then burying them in some other locations in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Army of Yugoslavia on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija never took part in digging up any dead bodies or transporting any dead bodies to other localities outside the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the basis for your confidence in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm certain of this on the basis of the counter-intelligence operation situation which I monitored daily in my units through my organs, and if something like that had happened, I would certainly have had to know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying only if it was something that happened at the instance of the army, or are you saying that if any group exhumed a number of bodies and transported them out of Kosovo that you would know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would know only if that happened in the presence of the army or with the participation of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, yesterday you told us -- tell me this: Mr. Djakovic came to the position of the operations officer in the Pristina Corps, and after that who replaced him? You say that in 1999 Mr. Radojko Stefanovic arrived. Up to that point in time, up to the arrival of Radojko Stefanovic, was somebody else the operations officer after Djakovic, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Colonel Djakovic left his duty in January 1999, I think, there was a period of time when there was no chief of the operative affairs department. This was rather the first desk officer, Colonel Ratko Tesovic, who was the acting officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Radojko Stefanovic, when he took over the duty of the operations organ of the Pristina Corps, did he attend meetings of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Radojko Stefanovic, as I said, went to see the MUP operations officer occasionally for them to coordinate actions that had to be carried out, but there was nothing like a Joint Command. Are you asking me about 1999? I don't know of the existence of any Joint Command at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, yesterday my learned friend Mr. Stamp showed you a document signed by Djindjic, and you explained what post he held. Are you aware whether your colleague from the 3rd Army, who was your superior in the professional sense, do you know whether he ever attended meetings of the Joint Command in 1999 [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1998, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998 I think once or twice, but I think it was only once actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that he might have learned some operative information at such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you, those were meetings where information was exchanged between the MUP, the state security, and the army concerning the current security situation. I assume he carefully listened to what the colleagues from the other domains said about the situation, and they listened to what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, my learned friend Mr. Stamp also asked you something about security for the meeting held on the 1st of June, 1999, and he asked you whether you knew about that meeting. My question is: The plan of providing security for the commander, to the best of your knowledge, is it made for each individual visit of his or trip or is it a long-term plan, created for a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the security department there was my assistant for staff security affairs, and it was his task to guide the work of the military police, to provide security for the facilities and persons who are entitled to security by law. The security plans are drawn up monthly and they are delivered to the battalion commander of the military police, who is to implement those plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We heard from many witnesses here, and you confirmed that in the Grand Hotel there was an information centre and a place where post was exchanged. Did this information centre and centre for the exchange of post, where strictly confidential documents also arrived, was it constantly guarded by the military police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in the course of the war the command of the Pristina Corps was dispersed in several locations outside Pristina. The only element that remained in the town itself, for a thousand reasons, was that information centre. And as there was a constant danger because terrorists entered the town itself dressed in civilian clothes, so there was a military police unit that was constantly guarding that information centre because we had to protect it from terrorist attacks. There were also two policemen there inspecting the mail to ensure there was no sabotage. This is also done in peacetime today at every point where post is received and sent out. There are always two policemen there to inspect the mail for possible sabotage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I wanted a shorter reply, so please try to be brief because our time is running out. So you were not at the meeting on the 1st of June, or rather, you said you were but had you not attended that meeting would you have learned later on that the meeting had been held, in view of the fact that the security plans are drawn up monthly?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P2945, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It's a newspaper article and my learned friend Mr. Stamp showed you a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before moving on, so I understand this last point fully. How is it you would learn later that the meeting had been held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that a security plan for security for the commander is drawn up, and the -- then this is reported and the reports came to me every morning concerning the problems of providing security for the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Reporting on the day before or on the plans for the day ahead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He reports on the previous day and on the plans for the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean there's a good chance you knew about the meeting before it took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking about the meeting in the Grand Hotel, it was held without previous notice because, as I learned, Mr. Sainovic arrived from Belgrade to inform us about the negotiations and how they were proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now see page 2 of this text. Could we zoom in on document number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, before we look at this document in detail, you're an officer with one of the highest ranks in the army and I'm sure you can tell us this. Whenever a document is sent to a subordinate command or to a superior command, the addressee, where according to the Rules of Service, on what part of the page, is the addressee mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Rules for Official Correspondence in the Army of Yugoslavia, the address to which an official army document is being sent is in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We've seen some documents where the addressee's also on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only telegrams sent to units have the addressee on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that the address of any command where the superior or subordinate is placed in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why then is this title "to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" in the middle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document was not sent to any institution or any command. It's a document given to an operations officer and it contains information on terrorist activities. It's not addressed to any institution or command, otherwise according to the rules it would have had to be placed in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And I will have only one more question. Yesterday my learned friend Mr. Stamp asked you more than once whether there was any commander who was held responsible for the crimes committed by his subordinates. As you were in the security organ, are you aware that the Yugoslav Criminal Code in 1999 contained the institute of command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not provided for in the law at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those were all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is Novica Stamenkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stamenkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stamenkovic.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please be so kind to introduce yourself for the record. Tell us your first and last name and your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Novica Stamenkovic, I was born on the 2nd of September, 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you give us some basic information about your military career.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the military academy for the ground forces, the traffic service, in 1972. The command staff school for tactics, I graduated from that in 1985, and then I went to the School of National Defence which I completed in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please be kind enough to tell us what was your last duty in the Army of Yugoslavia and when your service in the army terminated.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: My last duty was assistant commander of the 3rd Army for the rear, and it ceased on the 1st of January, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what is your status now?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: I am now a military pensioner, I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And your rank?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, what duties did you perform in the course of 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, I was the chief of the organ for operations and rear affairs in the organ for the rear of the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the duties of the organ at whose head you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The main competencies of that organ in 1998 and 1999 were the following: Operative and planning work in the organs for the rear, then monitoring and proposing of measures for the building up of combat-readiness of the rear units which by establishment were subordinated to the commander for the rear, this was the 549th Automobile Battalion, 186th technical centre, the Nis military medical centre, and units which by special orders were placed within the competence of the commander for the rear, the 201st and 202nd rear base and the Nis military hospital. And there was also another important competency, and that was coordinating the work of the organs in the rear and coordinating the rear organs with the other organs in the command of the army, and there were other tasks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't need the details, but just explain what rear security entailed.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Security of the rear was defined by the rules, two, in peacetime and in wartime, two rules, but the essence of all of them are is that there were measures and steps that the command staffs, administrations, and units of the army are engaged in, in order to in peacetime create conditions conducive to combat training and preparation for wartime, and in wartime to create conditions for the combat units to be as successful as possible in waging a national war of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to ask you for less theory and more specifics and practical facts, and tell us what the rear did.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: It was to supply the combat and non-combat units with food, to maintain vehicles and technical equipment in working order, health care and protection, veterinary care and protection, protection against fires, and any other special tasks needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us briefly how the rear security was organized of the 3rd Army in wartime?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the 3rd Army command -- the 3rd Army command was the protagonist of security for the rear in its area of responsibility for all army units and also for the units of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the command of the air force and anti-air defence in its own area. And in implementing the tasks, it relied on the central rear base of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the medical military academy, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you also rely on the capacities in the territory?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: In carrying out our tasks for rear security, we relied in part on the capacities of the territory or society, that is to say the railroads, the traffic and transport companies, the food producers, pharmaceutical producers, clothing manufacturers, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Because you needed to use the capacities that the state provided, was it necessary for the rear organs to cooperate with anyone in that respect?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: For the rear security to function successfully, it was indispensable to cooperate with all the organs of power and authority and the leaders of the companies I mentioned, companies that provided services or provided supplies for the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, these competencies and authorisations of the organs for rear security, were they regulated by law?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Defence regulated the competencies and authorisations of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia, and similarly the rights and duties of the organs of power and authority, the work organizations, and indeed individuals in offering services, providing services, and creating material conditions for the functioning of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any separate legal provisions or orders for situations to proclaim a state of war on the territory?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The Law on Defence defined the rights and duties of all the factors involved in the proclamation of a state of war and during a war itself, and we all adhered to those provisions, when the war started, or rather, the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia started. But the commanders of the units at the different levels of command from the army, the corps, via the brigades also issued their own orders and instructions regulating in greater detail the implementation of certain activities, rights, and duties in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, these orders, were they dovetailed with the Law on Defence?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: All orders were based on the Law on Defence, which was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Law on Defence is Exhibit P985, and the special orders that were issued on the basis of that law of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps are Exhibit 5D378 and 5D353. For us to move more speedily along, just for the record, I draw the Trial Chamber's attention to those documents without needing to pull them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, what was the organization of the rear security of the Yugoslav Army units in the area of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The army command, through its orders and chart for rear security, determined the protagonist of security in the Pristina Corps zone and the competence of those organs applied to establishment units of the Pristina Corps and the reinforce units sent to the Pristina Corps for the units of the anti-aircraft defence as well deployed in the Pristina Corps area, and for army units of the General Staff in that same zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which sources of supply for the Yugoslav Army units in Kosovo and Metohija existed during the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The sources of supply for the Yugoslav Army units in Kosovo and Metohija during the war were first and foremost their own reserves, the units' reserves, that is to say what we called wartime reserves; then transitory reserves in the garrisons and reserves of the superior commands and the reserves which were located on the territory, or rather, contracted quantities of produces which the producers sent to the rear security organs and also there was a commission for procurement and this was placed -- this was paid for at a lower level, or rather, at a local level on the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, what was the cooperation with MUP like in Kosovo and Metohija with respect to realizing the tasks of rear security?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the organs of the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija, the rear organs had to cooperate constantly and continuously. In the barracks in Kosovo and Metohija, there was separate premises for putting up MUP units, so it was logical for the rear security to act together. That is to say their food, water, washing of clothes, and so on, that's what it applied to. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that MUP facilities were built, whose facilities were they, military facilities or MUP?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: They were MUP buildings but within the barracks compounds, that means they weren't military facilities in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I interrupted you. You wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As for the organs of the rear, one of the main forms of cooperation with the MUP was to ensure the safety of movement and passage of vehicles, that was a joint task to ensure that the roads were open and traffic -- but traffic control came exclusively under the MUP organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, could you please slow down, Witness.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was necessary to provide security for the military columns and supply columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What measures were taken to ensure the successful functioning of security of the rear in Kosovo and Metohija during the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: When the competent authorities assessed that the attack on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was imminent, then the rear organs undertook a series of measures to ensure that it functioned properly during the war, and I'm going to mention some of those measures. First of all, accelerated maintenance and repair of all combat systems; second, replenishment with the proper cadres in all the units of the corps; next, all the combat devices were brought up to standard as well as the non-combat means, so that in the units, brigades, regiments, and so on, that we had a food reserve for 30 days and for separate units for a different period of time, tins and so on, which means that they could be independent if the food-chain were to be cut. Then we took another important measure, it was the dispersion and resettlement -- or relocation of material resources of the unit to avoid their destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, you're a traffic officer, an officer of the traffic service, and I'm interested in now to hear about the principles and ways in which motor vehicles and fuel supplies were regulated.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I say something about fuel supplies first. We had logistical bases to supply the units from their own warehouses which were in Prokuplje and Velika Grabovica, those two towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, your supplies, did they come from the fuel depot in Pristina, in Obilic, for example?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The Jugopetrol and Beopetrol fuel depots in Pristina and Obilic were civilian depots, and the army did not have direct cooperation with them because the logistics basis would get their fuel from the oil refinery in Pancevo, directly from the producers, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Colonel, something about the motor vehicles and how you had the necessary supply of motor vehicles and ensured it for the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Law on Defence, supplies for the army, replenishment of supplies, came from the army fund, 50 per cent, and 50 per cent were vehicles taken from the capacities of the territory, that is to say from work organizations and individuals. And that was how the Pristina Corps received its supplies and replenishment. The situation was more favourable with regard to some vehicles. From the army fund there was the heavy-duty vehicles mostly and trucks that did not exist on the territory, whereas the majority of heavy-duty and -- trucks and passenger vehicles were supplied by the defence ministry and their local branches, my mobilising the vehicles and replenishment to make the fund up to scratch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the law provided for a mobilisation plan for motor vehicles to be devised, taking them from companies and civilians alike?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The overall mobilisation plan meant replenishment of vehicles, and this was done in all the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In such cases, was compensation envisaged?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: For every vehicle that was recruited and used for the needs of the army or suffered damage, compensation was paid to the owner according to the regulations. There was a piece of legislation in place governing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What was the replenishment of vehicles in the Pristina Corps at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1999 the Pristina Corps had about 50 per cent of the vehicles it needed from the -- from one fund and 50 per cent from another. The army fund -- the corps was missing about 2.000 vehicles, rather, it was 232.000.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And 33 vehicles of various kinds. In the Pristina Corps the 201st rear base --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of institutions needed another 2.000 units so that the units in that area would have the required number of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little bit because we will have errors in the transcript. We already have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These figures need to be clarified. Can you deal with that, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please speak a little slower so that we don't have to go back again because then we waste a lot more time. I asked you what was the number of vehicles in the Pristina Corps at the beginning of the war. Could you please answer slowly.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1999, in the Pristina Corps, there were about 50 per cent vehicles from the army per cent and 50 per cent from the list fund. For a completely replenishment the Pristina Corps lacked about 2.000 vehicles, or more precisely, 2.033 vehicles, and about 2.000 vehicles were lacking for the units of the army and the air force and anti-aircraft defence on the territory of the Pristina Corps, which is a further 2.000 vehicles. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the needs, but what vehicles did they have?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The possibility of obtaining all this did not exist in Kosovo and Metohija, so the Pristina Corps from the list fund on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija secured only about 30 per cent of its own needs, and the remainder was on the so-called ex-territorial principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the list fund?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was trying to ask the witness to explain this, as we will move on to another topic after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please explain what the list fund is?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the list fund in military terminology means motor vehicles which under the Law on Defence working on organizations and individuals under the plan of the regional organs of the Ministry of Defence give to the army for the army's needs so the vehicles are used by the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, an earlier answer said there were 50 per cent vehicles from the army per cent and 50 per cent from the list fund, and now we hear that the list fund is what the army actually provide. It might have helped if you would get an answer to your original question which was: How many vehicles did the Pristina Corps have. Can you answer that in relation to early 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Pristina Corps in its composition had about 50 per cent of its establishment needs with military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, the number of vehicles, please. We don't know the establishment need. Just tell us the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The needs were 4.600-odd vehicles, whereas they had 2.100 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll break there for 20 minutes. Mr. Stamenkovic, we have to have a break at this stage. While we have that break, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamenkovic, before the break we started talking about motor vehicles. Some witnesses of the Prosecution spoke before this Tribunal about the theft and confiscation of civilian vehicles in Kosovo and Metohija by the army. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: I assert that as for organized theft, confiscation, looting, robbery, and so on of vehicles by the army, there was none of that. The army had its regular methods of obtaining vehicles. There may have been thefts of vehicles by individuals, but the competent organs always acted to prevent that and to prosecute the perpetrators. And such vehicles were always kept by the organs that were competent to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what happened to persons who were found to be in possession of such vehicles and who were members of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the Army of Yugoslavia who unlawfully took a vehicle from someone were arrested and prosecuted before the competent military courts, and the vehicles were confiscated from them and pursuant to decisions issued by the courts returned to their owners or otherwise disposed of as the court decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at Exhibit 5D189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before moving, is this an exhibit that relates to this subject, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the exhibit I have called up is an order issued by the corps commander for the use -- engagement and use of military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we do that. Mr. Stamenkovic, can you tell us how often orders were made returning vehicles that had been wrongly confiscated to their owners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with the occurrence of unlawful confiscation, commands at all levels including the corps command and the brigade command issued their own orders to prevent theft and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question. Please, just answer the question I've asked you. How many orders do you know of that were made returning vehicles to owners where these vehicles had been confiscated from them? We haven't seen any yet in this court, and I would like you to tell me about them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the commands of units cannot restore a wrong fully confiscated vehicle to its owner without a judicial decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you about. You told us there were decisions made by the courts returning vehicles to their owners. I want you to tell me about some of these. Let's put meat on the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to the best of my knowledge, up to the time of my retirement, about 70 per cent of all the vehicles that were found or confiscated were restored to their owners through decisions handed down by courts, but I cannot give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you actually know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I know of some examples. For example, a bus was restored to a privately owned company in Prizren which proved that it was the owner of the bus and the command of the 160th technical training centre was where the handover took place and the vehicle was restored to its owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when was it confiscated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1999, during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you said 70 per cent of all that had been confiscated were restored. How many does that amount to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 600-odd vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the type of confiscation, how he learned about it, I don't want to interrupt you but I was planning to ask about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have actually seen documents which give figures for confiscated vehicles I think, but I was concerned about this question of court orders which I don't think we've seen, but I may be wrong about that. If I am, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We did not see the court orders. I asked through the National Council to give us an overview of how many vehicles were restored by the courts, but I'm still waiting for that. We did apply to the National Council in October to get that information through the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, but this witness will testify to the best of his knowledge. I'll ask him about the types of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is an order of the corps commander dated the 12th of April. Can you explain to us what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This order was issued pursuant to a similar order delivered to the corps command from the army command, and it refers to the following: In order to properly use motor vehicles from the list, as they are no different from civilian vehicles, they have to be used according to certain rules, they have to be marked, they have to be used according to establishment, and those which are outside the system have to be deployed, secured, and guarded according to our military regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And can you briefly comment on items 6 and 8?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: In item 6 there is an order that all the motor vehicles recruited for the use of the Army of Yugoslavia have to have documents in good order, both for the vehicle and for the driver. And the organs of the military traffic police on all public roads and other areas where vehicles move would check this, and if there are individuals without the proper documents, they will be held responsible, and this would include criminal responsibility, arrest, and so on and so forth. Also, the commanders of units where officers and individuals use such vehicles would also be held responsible, certain command measures would be taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said in item 4 that all the vehicles had to be marked, the civilian licence plates were not to be removed, and they had to be specially marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now look at 5D1274.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this represents and what is usually entered into a form of this kind.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: As we can see on the screen, this is a sign which, according to the rules regulating the marking of motor vehicles in the army, was used to mark motor vehicles from the list which were used in the Army of Yugoslavia. And on that sign, along with the number of the military post or the unit to which it belonged, there also had to be a signature and a stamp of the unit commander so that this would be the only valid form. Because a sign is not a sign of belonging unless it is verified by a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The -- are these the orders of the corps commander and the subordinate commander, did they --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at 5D663.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- And I would like to know whether these orders were implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commanders of subordinate units issued their own orders. Here we see an order of the command of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade regulating the procedure when motor vehicles are confiscated, and he says specifically that all motor vehicles which are illegally obtained or were used by military persons but were the object of a crime have to be specially located and secured with guards from the unit. And for all such units records were kept and the superior command was informed, whereas only a military court at the Pristina Corps command could issue decisions on the use of these vehicles. Vehicles which were found on the roads also had to be specially marked and could not be used without special approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We'll come to that and we'll see what happened to motor vehicles which were found as opposed to those obtained through a criminal act. But was this order really implemented? Were special locations established where motor vehicles obtained through criminal actions were kept along with all the appropriate records?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When inspecting the units of the Pristina Corps, I noticed those parking lots, they really existed, there were various vehicles on them, they were guarded, and I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Exhibit 5D487, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you comment briefly on item 3(b). There seems to be a rather vigorous warning here for those who obtained vehicles through crimes. Can we see here any cases provided for under item 3 and why was this order issued?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 354th Brigade ordered in item 3, under (b), that motor vehicles and drivers without the proper documents should be detained and brought in, and that the most stringent measures should be taken against such drivers. This was done so that you could not find military vehicles that were improperly marked on the roads, especially not those obtained through criminal offences such as theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'll ask you now to look at 5D188, and using the example of this order let's try to have you explain what was understood by "found" and "confiscated" motor vehicles. Look at this order issued by the Pristina Corps command dated the 12th of April, 1999, and comment on item 4, please. Does this refer to vehicles which were obtained through a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Item 4 of this order says that all motor vehicles which were illegally obtained and used by military personnel and which constitute objects of a crime should be placed in a special parking area which shall be established and that this parking area shall be guarded by members of the military police units, and prescribed criminal documentation and records shall be kept for each vehicle, a copy of the documents shall be kept in the vehicle, these vehicles shall only be used pursuant to a decision of the Pristina military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Item 5 refers to found vehicles. Can you explain what found vehicles were?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to clarify this, I have to explain first what in our terminology was meant by "found vehicles." Found vehicles were all vehicles found on public roads or other areas of which the owner was unknown, the owner was not present, and they were obstructing traffic. These were found vehicles. Such vehicles were removed from the roads and a special parking area was established, also under guard, and these vehicles could be used only if they were needed by the unit to carry out its tasks, but by no means could they be used for private purposes. They were marked and they were used because -- to make up for the numbers missing of vehicles from the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Bonomy asked you: Can you tell me what was done with these vehicles after the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: After the end of the war, all mobilised motor vehicles, mobilised according to plan, were restored to their owners, who had been issued with the documents when the vehicles were handed over. So they were able to use these documents to retrieve their vehicles; if the vehicles had been damaged or destroyed, they were compensated. Those vehicles which were confiscated were kept in the units until the competent courts, whether civil or military, handed down the proper decisions on what should be done with those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why, Colonel, were these vehicles not left in Kosovo and Metohija when the army and the police retreated from Kosovo, when they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the army and MUP withdrew from the area of Kosovo and Metohija, the vehicles could not be left behind because the civilian authorities were not functioning and there were no organs, even the UNMIK police was not functioning then, so there was nobody to whom the documentation should -- could be left and units would then have a proper way of relieving themselves of that responsibility. So they took the vehicles with them. Some of those vehicles were restored to their owners from the new locations if the owners were able to prove that they were the owners or if the courts handed down the appropriate decision. For example, there was a work organization Binacka Morava from Gnjilane and their vehicles were restored in the Vranje garrison where the units that had those had been relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have already said here that the Defence applied to the General Staff level to get this data through the cooperation council, but what I want to know is how you know this information you're giving us now.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you, until the 1st of January, 2003, I was assistant commander for the rear, the traffic service as part of the rear organ was subordinated to me, they kept these records, so I know that from their reports, and that's why I have this information. When the army command started to be disbanded, the problem of the restoration of vehicles were handed over to the traffic administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, so I don't have the final numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, but my colleague Mr. Petrovic has just arrived from Belgrade and has joined us here in the courtroom, and we were told that quite soon we would have through the National Council this exhibit, and I'll then put it on the bar table and ask that it be introduced through the bar table. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, as assistant commander for the 3rd Army of the rear, did you know the rear organs for the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer of the traffic service, for many years I was in the rear organs, especially as assistant for the rear, and I knew almost all the officers in the rear who occupied leading posts. For example, in the Pristina Corps the assistant for the rear, he was Colonel Petrovic, I knew him, and the chief of the technical service, Colonel Brankovic the medical corps, Rankovic. Well, I knew them for 15 or 16 years and as far as the chief of the traffic service is concerned, Colonel Simunovic, I have known him for 25 or 26 years, so I knew people who occupied leadership positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you cooperate with these people during the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
