utterances.text: I did cooperate with these people, both before the war and during the war so that cooperation was on a continuous basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know an officer from the procurement department of the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The procurement department in the organs for the rear of the Pristina Corps -- that doesn't exist. A long time ago in 1985 or 1986, these procurement departments in the army were abolished and were never established anymore. The only thing that existed was the administration for procurement and military equipment and were attached to the Ministry of Defence and nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, we have heard witness Lakic Djorovic testify here, and in his testimony and statement to the Prosecution he mentioned an officer by the name of Tijanic from the procurement department of the Pristina Corps. Did you know somebody with that name?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Tijanic, and being in a procurement department which does not exist of the Pristina Corps and it never existed, ever since the Pristina Corps was under the 3rd Army command, and that is since 1988, so never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell us, or rather, explain to us more precisely the way in which donations were used, gifts, and other things of that nature, and were there any cases of that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: There were donations, there were gifts from the territory, and upon the arrival of those resources to the units, this is what was done. A commission could take them on, then they would be checked to see that they were in proper order, and then they were recorded and placed in depots and warehouses and used like any other devices for the replenishment of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia, did it apply confiscation or requisitioning of resources in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Although those methods are provided for in the Law on Defence, the Yugoslav Army did not use that; it used capacities from the territory exclusively through the competent organs in Kosovo and Metohija, this was the provincial executive -- Temporary Executive Council so that there was no need to resort to that, although it was provided for by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you explain to us the notion and concept of war booty.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The term war booty implies resources which arrived in army units through combat. At the end of combat, when the battle-field was checked and investigated, different things were found, weapons, medicines, clothing, weapons, and whole depots and warehouses of the terrorists in Kosovo, so that was considered war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's look at 5D186 together now, please, and then you can tell us whether this is an example of the corps command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. Bakrac. I'd like to go back to page 46, lines 23 to 25 -- I'm sorry, page 45, lines 23 to 25, when you asked about the witness Lakic Djorovic and what he testified concerning an officer by the name of Tijanic from the procurement department of the Pristina Corps. Did you know somebody with that name? I'm not certain that the answer given appropriately addresses the question which you had posed of the witness, so I would not mind if you could get a more precise answer from him for my understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I'll do my best to get a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, I don't want to repeat all this, but a witness said here in court something. Now, in the Pristina Corps was there a procurement department, did that ever exist?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the Pristina Corps was there any individual in charge of procurement of any type and whose name was -- or whose surname was Tijanic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether that suffices?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't I think really complete the answer. Did you know someone in the corps called Tijanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I wanted us to look at 5D186 now, and I'd like to have your comments to item 1 and tell me whether the corps command regulated the way in which war booty was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The corps command and all the units in depth regulated the way in which war booty was collected and in item 1 it says: "Every unit the size of a brigade regiment form a commission for collecting war booty, which will conduct inspection and identification and make an inventory and record of the assets seized."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And was that what was done?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively, that was precisely what was done with war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, now sanitization of the terrain, "asanacija," does that come within the remit of the rear security?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: When I spoke about the organs which I headed, I spoke about special activities and the sanitization of the terrain is comprised there because the law -- the regulation which determines sanitization was compiled by the administration of the General Staff, so yes, that does come within its competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what sanitization of the terrain actually means, its importance and significance?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The sanitization of the terrain implies and incorporates giving assistance to any wounded persons left in the terrain; then to uncover, identify, bodies, the bodies of those killed in order that they be buried; then doing away with anything that is -- presents a danger to humans and animals to ensure that the terrain is sanitary and that life can evolve in the terrain. So the object of sanitization is to find any people who might be wounded and give assistance; then to find dead bodies in order to be able to bury them and identify them; and to protect the living environment, that is to say to protect the units, the people, the population, and the general environment to keep it healthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the 3rd Army and in the Pristina Corps, how was sanitization regulated, matters of sanitization?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Army command in the Pristina Corps, sanitization was regulated on a basis of a number of orders. Orders and instructions were issued for sanitization to take place on the basis of the guide-lines and instructions that I just explained to you in my earlier answer, and it specifies the duties and obligations in conducting sanitization. The order was that sanitization in the border belt, for example, should be conducted exclusively by the units of the Yugoslav Army as well as in their areas of deployment, that sanitization in the rest of the terrain should be conducted by the powers of authority and the MUP in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the exhibits that relate to regulating this are 5D346, it is an order from the 3rd Army command; 5D347; 5D352, orders by the Pristina Corps; 52633 [as interpreted]; and 5D179, also from the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, how did the Pristina Corps command gain an insight into the orders given for sanitization and whether they were carried out?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps formed a very professional team to exercise control and give assistance to units in carrying out sanitization so that the commission in question sent regular reports to the corps command about how sanitization was going on in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, let us now take a look together at Exhibit 5D203, and may we have your comments -- well, it's an order from the command of the Pristina Corps dated the 20th of April, 1999. Is it an order which sets out the people making up the commission -- so may we have comments on item 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said the corps commander issued an order by which he set up a team to control the sanitization of the battle-field, and from the team composition we can see that there was an investigating judge there; there was a professional man, a pathologist; there was the crime technician whose name is not mentioned here because they were the people who were on duty; and there was a veterinary technician because of the livestock in the battle-field, so they were in charge of implementing the work. Now, item 2, paragraph 2, says exactly what I said earlier on, that the units were in charge of sanitization in the border belt after combat operations and the zone of combat operations in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, you said that within the frameworks of sanitization all types of weapons and lethal objects and anything that presented a danger to life in the environment was seen to. Now, the Pristina Corps, did it take any measures to protect the environment?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, not linked to sanitization orders were issued radioactive -- radioactivity was measured through Kosovo and Metohija, things like that, regardless of who the facilities belonged to that were attacked by NATO's air force in order to protect the units and also to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So were these measurements taken on civilian facilities as well?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, an example being private houses, bridges, refugee camps, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, P -- 5D402 is an exhibit relating to that, the radiological measurements that were undertaken, and in that sense I'd like us to look at the following exhibit, it's a Defence Exhibit 5D1152, and this is a document from the command of the 52nd artillery and rocket --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Earlier you gave us a list of numbers to which you were referring. It was 5D347, 5D352, orders by the Pristina Corps; and then you referred to 5D633. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2633, P2633.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: P2633 is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, let us take a look at 5D1152 now, please. It's a document of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade. Tell me if you know what this is about; and if you do, please may we have your comments to the document.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this document is familiar. It is a report of the commander of the 52nd anti-aircraft defence artillery brigade of the 23rd of April, 1999, in which he informs that during regular sanitization and control of the terrain his team for measuring radioactivity established that the -- in 10 tonnes of flour found in the basement of a house in Osek Hilja some 3 kilometres from Djakovica flour was found with higher of radiation with between 1 and 3 milligray per hour and for that type of food stuff, 2 milligray per hour is the permissible limit. And that the food was transported by the Mother Teresa humanitarian organization for feeding the local population, which was predominantly Albanian population. Measurement was taken for the 3 tonnes of flour which had already been issued to bakeries for private bread production that bread baking should be stopped and the flour was taken away and the necessary documents compiled and the situation was, if I can say, sanitized or dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me who -- what ethnicity the baker was and what population did they cater to.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a local baker, Albanian, and there were no Serbs in that village, it was all local Albanian inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, you told us that the medical corps was something that was dealt with by the rear. Now, do you know whether the medical battalion, medical battalion of the Pristina Corps, whether it provided assistance to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that it did so in a number of cases, I know of a case where there was a surgical intervention, surgery performed on two Albanians and assistance given for eight babies and treated a number of other people, and I do know that. And I happen to know that because I as the assistant, or rather, the chief of the organ for operative rear affairs with the Supreme Command, I toured the battalion and Colonel Visic reported to us about those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did you tour the battalion?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: We toured the battalion towards the end of May 1999 around Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your rear organs, did they provide other forms of assistance to the civilian population as well; and if so, could you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to orders from the superior command, all possible assistance was to be given to refugees, and I know the example of the 37th Motorised Brigade, who in its area of responsibility, the Srbica area, gave the population assistance in food, it provided flour to bake bread for the refugees. I also know of another case when the 549th Brigade in the village of Ljubizda near Prizren helped the civilian population by handing out food to them and giving medical assistance as well to anybody who was sick in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, in view of the fact that you led the rear organ, as an organ of the rear do you know that the Army of Yugoslavia gave over some of its resources to the Ministry of the Interior; and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. The Army of Yugoslavia -- I know that the Army of Yugoslavia, or rather, the 3rd Army gave to the MUP organs 35 non-combat vehicles of the TAM type, T-A-M type. The order was received from the General Staff and those vehicles were handed over from the army units outside the Pristina Corps, because the Pristina Corps was in the focus of our attention so that the Pristina Corps command was not informed of that. Anyway, these vehicles we handed over, as provided for by the rules and regulations. We took off the military licence plates, and then the MUP would put their own on and use it for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know whether any combat resources were handed over?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure was properly similar via the General Staff for the combat systems and resources, but since that didn't come under the rear organs, it was the administration of the branches and services in the Army of Yugoslavia, so I don't know about that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The command of the 3rd Army during the war, did it compile a schematic for rear security, and what did this chart refer to?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the war, I think it was the 4th of April, when a new schematic was compiled for rear security and for all the army units, and it was sent to the Pristina Corps, and I personally compiled that chart, and it referred exclusively to the Pristina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you include reinforcements for the Pristina Corps in that chart?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The reinforcements were entered in and then the kind of reinforcements and number of men, and this was updated regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In that chart of rear security, were structures outside the Army of Yugoslavia included?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no structures outside the army were included in that chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware that at one point in April an order arrived on the resubordination of the MUP to the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As you were the author of that chart, that chart of the rear security, the numbers and the materiel resources that had to be delivered, was it updated after the order on resubordination?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no need because as far as I know the MUP units were not resubordinated to the army at all, and I would have to know that precisely in order to obtain both combat and non-combat needs for those units, for all resubordinated units that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would somebody else do that or would you have had to do that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would have had to be me because I was the author or my organs, but with my knowledge and under my supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those were all my questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Any other cross-examination by Defence counsel? None. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. Where were you based during the war in 1999 from March to June 1999?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war from March I was in the command of the 3rd Army, but very often I spent time on the territory of the Pristina Corps at the army forward command post or in the corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So where was the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 3rd Army was in Nis and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So -- and how often would you go to the territory of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: On the average, once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you participate in any of the operations or activities to clean up territory after combat or after army manoeuvres?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. That was done by organs from my services, but not I personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You went and you conducted inspections at various army posts; is that it?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and to provide assistance, inspections and providing assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When -- or if the army located bodies of persons appearing to be civilians that are unidentified, would the army be involved in the burial of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: That would depend on the area where they were. If the bodies were in the border belt, then the army investigating organs and the teams for sanitization would participate in that, and then civilian authorities would also be involved in that. But if it was outside the border belt, all that would be done by the civilian authorities and the army would not participate, it would simply inform the civilian authorities that the bodies had been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the army maintain a log of unidentified persons that it had buried or records, not necessarily a log, but records; and if so, where would those records be kept?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was done. I can give you an example. The village of Slomine [phoen] in Glogovac municipality, for example, when a team, the military investigating judge, pathologists, military police, forensic technicians, and so on found a grave with 16 corpses. They processed them, identified them, handed them over to the authorities for burial and instituted criminal proceedings against unknown perpetrators before the criminal court in Pristina and there are quite a few other examples of the same kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were the records in respect to these corpses kept?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: They were in sometimes, or rather, in the former military courts previously, but now in the military parts of courts, whatever it's called now, but anyway the competent part of courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about some 800 corpses that General Pavkovic, the 3rd Army commander, claimed -- I'm sorry, is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Were you asked at any time to send out teams to do investigations in respect to corpses numbering around 800 by the 3rd Army commander or by the 3rd Army commander or organs of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first, this number, the number 800, is not familiar to me, it's not what I know. And there were requests by the commander of the Pristina Corps and the army command teams were sent to carry out sanitization, as far as I know, in seven locations, for a total number of about 208 bodies that had been found. I know that from the reports of the teams who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Did you know one Lakic Djorovic? He was an officer in the Pristina Corps command, a prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Personally, no. I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting on the 24th of November, 1999, the topic of which was dealing with vehicles or -- I withdraw the question. Did you attend a meeting in respect to vehicles that had been seized in Nis on the 24th of November, 1999?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there another Colonel Stamenkovic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a Stamenkovic, but he's not a colonel, he's a lieutenant-colonel in Nis in the traffic service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You said that there were -- there was no procurement department in the Pristina Corps command. I would like you to look at a document, and maybe you could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could P2762 be placed on the -- on e-court. And I would respectfully request the leave of the Court just to show him one small part of that document. It was not listed, Defence is not objecting, so I suppose I could proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at that, please, and also look -- if you could go to the last page of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a record of information provided to us by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia on the 28th of November, 2006, in which it says that: "A person other than Tijanic served as a technical procurement reserve officer for the Pristina Corps command ..." If you look at that, would you agree it's possible that even if there was not a department labelled the technical procurement department, there was an organ responsible for procurement in the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In the organs for the rear, in the rear services, there was never a single person dealing with procurement. For example, in the technical service the person who has to procure reserve parts is the one who has to maintain vehicles, he's the one who gets reserve parts. The person dealing with weapons obtains spare parts for weapons, but that was not within the competence of the Pristina Corps; it was within the competence of the army and the General Staff. The Pristina Corps could only ask, it could not procure. This was done by the rear bases, the army command, but it was not done by the Pristina Corps because the Pristina Corps was not authorised by establishment to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, was there such an officer, such a position as technical procurement reserve officer for the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was the chief of the technical service, the clerk for weapons, the clerk for motor vehicles, the clerk for communications, and another one, and those were all the organs in the Pristina Corps. Not a single one was for procurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what the one VTK log-book is?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the military territorial command, according to the abbreviation given here, but I'm not aware where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says here also that there are numerous individuals listed in the records with the last name Tijanic. Is it possible that there was a reserve officer in the Pristina Corps command by that name that you do not know?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible there is someone I didn't know, but he was not in the organs for the rear, and the organs for the rear were competent to procure materiel for the corps. I should have known about him or at least heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now we're dealing with this document, just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you were shown VTK. Is that a log-book of the corps or of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: Of the Ministry of Defence, not the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamenkovic, you told us that in 1998 and 1999 you were chief of the organ for operations and rear affairs and the organ for the rear of the command of the 3rd Army. And then when you retired in 2003, you were assistant commander of the 3rd Army for the rear. Which of these is the most -- which of these is the most senior position?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA STAMENKOVIC
utterances.text: The most senior position in the hierarchy is assistant commander of the 3rd Army for the rear. In 1998 and 1999 I was the deputy assistant commander for the rear, and then in 2001, I was appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamenkovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You can now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, who is next?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, suddenly things have speeded up. Our next witness is Dragisa Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for the witness to come in, Your Honours, we have changed the manner of testifying. This witness will be 92 ter and a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've said before that I certainly find difficulty with the concept of a 92 ter witness. What you have here is a witness, part of whose evidence is going to be presented in writing in terms of Rule 92 ter, but he's no more dead than any other witness who comes in and speaks to us. So we're grateful to you for making use of the provisions of Rule 92 ter to expedite the present of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the e-court number for the statement, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1379, Your Honour, 5D1379. I think the English version has the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marinkovic, good evening.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For the purposes of the transcript, please introduce yourself, tell us your first and last name, and your date, year, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragisa Marinkovic. I was born on the 23rd of April, 1947, in the village of Vrbovo in Vladicin Han municipality in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, on the 6th of December of this year, did you give to the Defence of General Lazarevic a statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of perusing that statement in detail?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does the statement express everything you told the Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you today those same questions, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you please make pauses between my question and your answer, although they're brief answers, but please remember to do that, pauses between my question and your answer to facilitate the work of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender into evidence the statement of this witness, 5D1379.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, since you gave the statement, we have it on e-court, all of us can read it, it's accessible to one and all and we can interpret what it says there. I'm just going to ask you a few additional questions. So there's no need for us to repeat all the things that are contained in the statement. What I'm interested in is to deal with one more topic, and that is the question of cooperation with the OSCE mission and the Pristina Corps command. Now, Colonel, is it true and correct that after you -- the OSCE mission arrived in Kosovo and Metohija you were in the team of the Pristina Corps for liaising with the mission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in the Pristina Corps team and I was the deputy leader of the team, Colonel Milan Kotur was deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly the ways in which this cooperation evolved, that is to say between the Pristina Corps and the OSCE mission and cooperation with the verifiers as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That cooperation was based on an agreement which our government had signed as well as on orders from the superior commands of the 3rd Army and the General Staff of the army. And almost on a daily basis meetings were held between the liaison team and the liaison officer with the verifiers of the OSCE mission to discuss certain issues, first and foremost troop movements, border issues, exercise and training, verifying the terrorist attacks, touring Albanian villages, and all other matters and issues that needed to be discussed at the request of one or at the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've been told that there's an error in the transcript, but we'll solve it more simply in asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you Milan Kotur's deputy or was he your deputy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was Milan Kotur's deputy. He was the leader of the team of the Pristina Corps for liaising with the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, in all the units of the Pristina Corps was there a liaison officer with the verifiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, pursuant to an order of the Pristina Corps, who was General Pavkovic at the time, according to the garrison principle there were liaison officers appointed for liaising with the OSCE mission; and in addition to that, all three border battalions had their own liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, the verifiers of the OSCE mission, could they enter the border belt?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they could, certainly. They could enter but respecting certain provisions, that is to say that they had to announce their arrival 24 hours ahead of time, and this is a provision which always -- was always in force for the border belt regime. So if they announced their arrival on time, that would be fine. There are many other things that took place. There were ambushes, because there was a special regime that applied to the border belt to prevent anything untoward from happening. So the rules had to be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, is there a document about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to call up on e-court a document, it is 5D1227, which speaks of -- well, before I do that I'm going to ask a question and then we can look at the document together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were the verifiers allowed to visit Albanian villages in the border belt?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, they were given permission to do that if they respected the rules and announced it in advance. There were no problems in their visiting the border villages, or rather, villages in the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have 5D1227, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a document from the command of the 57th Border Battalion. Can you give us your comments on point 8.5, item 8.5.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, item 8.5 says that on the 14th of March, 1999, in the Globocica sector, three members of the OSCE with a vehicle registration number, et cetera, manned by the following individuals requested permission to visit the villages of Gorance, Globocica, Kotlina, Dragomance, and Straza, and they were granted permission to visit, so there were no problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We see that it is a document from the border battalion, and these are villages unless I'm mistaken which are located in the border belt; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at another exhibit, 5D1228, and it would appear that in this document your name is mentioned. It's a document from a border battalion once again I believe -- yes, the 57th Border Battalion again, dated the 18th of March. Are you familiar with this document, or rather, do you know what it's about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It -- I am familiar with this document, and it says here that I gave permission for entry to an International Red Cross team which was supposed to control and see how humanitarian aid was being handed out and distributed. But there wasn't time to do that. I wanted to be cooperative, I gave permission, although they didn't announce it sufficiently in advance. They finished the job, but the commander of the border battalion reacted to this. I was remiss because I wanted to show goodwill to cooperate. Now, luckily nothing happened. It was a little unpleasant, the vehicles were not announced, anything could have happened, but luckily it didn't. I was told off, but the whole matter passed, and I'm happy to have helped the people out not to let them wait another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said something could have happened. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Because the border belt regime is a specific regime. There are ambushes, things can happen, and there's certain rules that must be respected in order to provide safety for everyone. So you must be given enough time to prevent anything, you must meet the team, escort them, provide for their security and safety, that kind of thing, which requires advance notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If vehicles have not been announced, can they move around the border belt?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it would be dangerous. So the vehicles and people must be identified. Nobody wants anything to happen, but if it is night-time or if there is a fog, and you can't identify the vehicles it can be very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We saw that the verifiers visited Albanian villages. The locals in these Albanian villages, did they complain to the verifiers about the conduct of the Army of Yugoslavia and its members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the reports from the border battalions, and in talking to the verifiers, they did not have any complaints about the behaviour and conduct of the army and soldiers in that border belt, quite the contrary. Those soldiers had lived there with those people for many years, and they gained their trust and confidence, and this was spread and so there wasn't -- there weren't any problems. And even the people from the OSCE missions occupying higher posts, they gave recognition to the army for its behaviour and conduct, they commended it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, whenever I was able to I did attend those meetings, and I know first-hand that that's how things stood. Those meetings were mostly led by Colonel Kotur, but in his absence I would stand in and chair the meetings. So whenever possible, I did attend the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Kotur. Was Colonel Kotur replaced from that post or was there some reorganization that took place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Colonel Kotur was not replaced. We were in a specific situation and the team, both the verifiers -- well, mostly we didn't know English, none of us knew English, and that was a handicap for the team so that there was the need of having officers come in who knew English; and so that happened I think sometime at the beginning of March, thereabouts. So it wasn't any question of replacement or anything like that. Colonel Kotur performed his duty in a very proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you still some more questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, two more documents and a few more questions, 10 to 15 minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marinkovic, we need to have a break at this stage; while we have it, would you leave the courtroom, please, with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, I just have a few more questions and two exhibits to look at. Tell me this, please, General Lazarevic, when he became commander of the Pristina Corps in January 1999, did he - and when I say "you," I mean your team - did he make suggestions with respect to the cooperation with the OSCE mission and the verifiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, not only did he make suggestions but the he asked that we inform him about our work. He was often in a situation whereby he was able to follow our work, and sometime in the second half of February he scheduled a preparation for the team with the verifiers, preparation session; and he personally chaired that. So he felt the need personally to indicate how the team could work in future, and he required a certain amount of flexibility in the work too. The verifiers' team -- he asked that the verifiers be allowed everything that they requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's look at 5D651, please, on e-court, and let's take a look at page 6, item 3 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Item 3, second paragraph in item 3. Is that what you were testifying about? It says on the 25th, in the Pristina Corps command a meeting was held with the liaison officers of all the garrisons except the Pec garrison and border battalions. The meeting was chaired by the command of the Pristina Corps, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that that is what I was talking about, so it was incorporated into the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you take part or were personally present during those preparations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember I was there, and I remember two particular things that the commander insisted upon. One was a spirit of cooperation, and he asked at the meeting and before that, that care and attention be paid to protecting the lives of the verifiers because they were, after all, in a situation in which they had to go to danger zones and the state provided guarantees, and it would be a very bad thing if anything untoward were to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's now take a look at 5D1226. And while we're waiting for that exhibit, please tell us whether after this meeting and the suggestions made by the corps commander, whether cooperation with the mission was promoted.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite obviously it was promoted, that was evident, and it was felt not only in our work but at the meetings also that took place with the verifiers of the OSCE mission, where they expressed their satisfaction at the fact that the cooperation was better with more participation and understanding all-round.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We see the composition of the team here. Look at paragraph 1, read out the first sentence there, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It said: "The OSCE representatives expressed their satisfaction with the cooperation and the changes in the approach to the mission by the organs and units of the Army of Yugoslavia. They noted that the problem of access to the border crossings had been resolved and that communication had been established between the mission and the liaison officers, which guaranteed cooperation. They requested a map with a 5-metre [as interpreted] border zone marked in" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you. So those were the results?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and those results set in very quickly when all the liaison officers -- well, the order was received rapidly and everything evolved according to the instructions given by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, the OSCE mission, did it control armaments in the units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The mission did control weapons, effect weapons controls according to an agreement, and we hardly had any problems there at all, that is to say weapons control was 100 per cent without any objections made or any complaints. I remember some figures, some statistics. Perhaps I won't be precise enough, but there were over 30 verifications of weapons conducted by the mission, although I'm not quite sure of the figures. I might have got them wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that completes my additional questioning. What I meant to say when I said "additional," I said questions outside the 92 ter statement. That's what I meant to say, not as additional examination or re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. It appears no Defence counsel wish to cross-examine. You will now be cross-examined on behalf of the Prosecutor by Ms. Carter. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As the Court indicated, my name is April Carter, and I'm here to ask you questions on behalf of the Prosecution. I have a few topics that I would like to discuss with you, the first of which is the criminal activity that was alleged by the VJ. Specifically in a number of the documents that were presented in your package, there are notations of MUP committing crimes and the concerns that the VJ had against that. What I would like to discuss is actually the reverse. Sir, when war began, how often were the units being inspected by the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, the units of the Pristina Corps took up their wartime positions in the deployment areas and principally with the aim of protecting themselves and the population. In that sense, right at the beginning, the Pristina Corps command exercised control or inspected, as you say here, the command officers carried out inspections and reported back on the state of affairs, they reported back about the situation they had found in the units. And this inspection did not only take place when the war began. I remember very well an order from the command of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic, which, or rather, several orders that are easily remembered. He said, Not two days must go by without the unit being inspected. We had assistance there from the command of the 3rd Army. We were helped out in that. They also conducted inspection and control. Representatives of the General Staff, the General Staff team, and also the forward command post of the 3rd Army was in Pristina and it was very valuable, because faced with that kind of situation they behaved -- well, they helped the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. So you say --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: -- That was very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said initially that the commanders were to inspect at least every other day and then there was some additional oversight. What I want to specifically focus on is either at the Pristina Corps level or at the 3rd Army level. When and how often did either the Pristina Corps or 3rd Army review or inspect the individual units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The collegium of commanders that were held, they were held on a daily basis, but not in its full composition because the corps command was never able to be in one place, but the succus [phoen] was there and the commander would call in others. But tasks were issued on the basis of a report from the unit and controls and inspections of certain units were decided upon, where the situation was urgent and most difficult and most necessary. So all the units, there were units where there were no terrorist activities in the Kosovsko Pomoravlje area, whereas the units in Metohija hardest hit, and that's where inspection was necessary, not only inspection but assistance as well. There were units who had come in from other parts to a terrain they weren't well-acquainted with and they had -- well, it was wartime and they had to gain our trust.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And the reason I'm asking is because we have seen a document in this case, P1996, which purports to be minutes from the MUP on 7 May of 1997 -- excuse me, 1999, and in it, it indicates rampant criminal activity by the VJ. And in fact, there was a meeting that was held between the top VJ officials and agreement of measures were to be taken. Specifically I want to know how the corps addressed the fact that reports were being sent in saying that in Pristina the military is not taking sufficient measures and most crimes are being perpetrated by the VJ, indicated problems with your volunteers, so that the VJ is driving around in civilian vehicles, the VJ refuses to stop at check-points and is threatening the MUP with weapons, military investigative judges are refusing to do on-site investigations. This is all being reported --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, could you just slow down a bit, please. It's very difficult for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to object because my colleague Ms. Carter says reports sent to the army. This is the minutes of the meeting at the MUP staff, and this witness had nothing to do -- has nothing to do with that. It's no report that was sent out. It's just a meeting held at the MUP staff, MUP headquarters, where there were no army representatives present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, might I just be allowed to add this. When Lazarevic, the accused Lazarevic, testified, he wasn't given permission to comment on these minutes precisely because it had nothing to do with the army, and he wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would respectfully direct counsel's attention to page 10 in the English, page 8 in the B/C/S, that indicates that there was a meeting held with top VJ officials, agreeing on the measures to be applied, but that they were not sufficient at the moment, so there appears to be a communication between the VJ and the MUP and that's the basis of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is this on the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On page 10, the very first line: "A meeting was held with VJ top officials at which it was agreed that measures" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I do apologise. "... But that they were not sufficient at the moment." And in Vasiljevic's own statement it discuses meetings happening thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's first establish from the witness what he knows about reports from the MUP about VJ criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware -- I listed out a number of accusations that were being placed at the feet of the MUP in Pristina by the Pristina secretariat. Did you receive any information about any of these allegations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid that I won't be of much use to you because it was my duty to mention that with regard to my functional duties as assistant commander for information and morale -- well, that's a specific sphere of activity, and never -- I never looked at a single document which related to meetings either with the MUP or anything in connection to the MUP, nor did I ever go to a single MUP unit. So my preoccupations were as follows: Information; the corps compositions, internally and externally; informing the public; monitoring and keeping morale at a high level in the units and commands; then cultural issues and entertainment; and the nurturing of traditions and tradition values, that was my remit. And pursuant to requests from the commander I would tour our units if the commander thought that I would be useful there so that I could provide him with the proper information to see how far the unit had come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we understand what your job was. Ms. Carter, please try to confine the witness to answering questions that are going to advance our knowledge on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And you indicated that you were dealing with the monitoring and the morale. There was a number of documents that were submitted with your package that indicate that you were concerned about the appearance of the troops, about some of the criminal activity that was noted in those documents. So was it part of your job to address what was happening in the specific units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, information and morale. Now, pursuant to a task issued by the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I can't allow you to do this. I want you to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you just tell me that as part of your duties with regards to the morale, the monitoring in the morale, was it part of your job to address the problems within the individual VJ units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to what issues?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In many of the documents that are attached to your 92 ter there's concerns of lack of appearance, of them going off without permission, of criminal activity, of any number of things. Was that part of your job, to oversee and to deal with the inspections of those issues?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In the description of my work post and my functional duties --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: -- but pursuant to a task issued by the commander, yes, so in this specific case, yes, and on a specific topic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So when you were reviewing the units, while there are concerns that are noted from external sources, that did not fall under your job description; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move to another topic, specifically the inspections that do appear to be part of your concerns. A number of documents that were provided with your package with regards to the 175th, specifically that the soldiers were leaving sectors, they were firing for no reason, and actually disciplinary actions had to be taken against that unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the 175th Motorised Brigade is concerned, sometime in the second half of April, there was several complaints with respect to the conduct of that unit; and the corps commander sent me with a team to size-up the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at that unit, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: What every officer needs to see is order and discipline, whether that exists, which also boosts morale and combat-readiness of the unit and the appearance of the unit in general --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and what did you see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I see. Well, what I saw is this, under the Mucibaba pass, I saw part of the unit and there was one soldier that was bordering on the positive, and part of the unit of volunteers who did not come up to standard, did not fulfil the norm with respect to their appearance and conduct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. That leads me to two questions. First, you used the term "a unit of volunteers." Are you telling me that there -- that entire unit was made up of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a group which was not deployed at the time in the various localities, formation-wise. Most of the volunteers in the wartime units were placed in localities, whether the signalsman was in the signals position, the artillery man in the artillery position, but with this group that was not the case --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can please just confine your answers to the questions I asked. I want to know about this group, so you said it was a not a group that was deployed at the time in various localities. I'm not certain I understand that. The group that you came upon that was being identified as the 175th. Are you saying that that entire group was made up of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a group of some 30-odd fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And when you say that they appeared -- they had bad appearance, can you please describe for us what you were seeing. And the reason I'm asking is many of our crime base witnesses have indicated that they saw soldiers in varying uniforms, beards, looking very shabby, that type of thing. And so I want to know from your perspective when you came across the soldiers what did you see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, when an officer arrives, he looks to see whether it was a well-ordered unit, whether there was order in it and security; and at that point in time, this unit was not secured. And what characterizes every unit if it is in defence, it must have security so that it cannot be taken by surprise and killed, that's the first point --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could help us by speaking in simple language that lay people would understand about what you observed there about the state of these people. Just tell us about it. In your statement you already said that this led to the commander and the Chief of Staff losing their jobs, based on your observations. Now, what did you actually see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm afraid that what was in the statement was not properly understood. On the basis of my report and the previous reports about that unit, what happened was that the corps commander inspected it and the army commander inspected it so that they could confirm whether reports that had been sent out about that unit were correct; and this led to the fact that they replaced on the spot the commander of that brigade, the Chief of Staff, and 15 officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we just helped out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But please -- you understand what I'm asking. Just tell us what the condition of these men was, what it was they were either doing or what their appearance was like that led you to report back and caused the corps commander and 3rd Army commander to carry out their own inspection. And don't complicate it with technical army language; just give us the facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their appearance was not soldierly, Your Honour, they didn't look like soldiers. They weren't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what did they look like --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- well-kept, neat. A soldier has to be wearing prescribed uniforms from head to toe. If they don't have the proper uniform, if they're shabby, if they have bits and pieces of clothing, this will not meet the inspecting officer's requirements. So if -- and if there's nobody in command, then you can expect bad things to happen. So I could not do otherwise but to report back about the appearance of this unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if you refuse to answer our questions and make a real effort to do so we shall just ignore all your evidence. You've told me nothing in answer to that question. I want you to tell us what they actually were doing that was wrong. I don't want you to tell me that if they aren't wearing the right uniform they will not meet the inspecting officer's requirements. I want to know what they were wearing and what they were doing that was offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was there, they were not doing anything, that's the thing, the unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's move on then. Ask another question, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You said they weren't doing anything, but can you confirm to me, when you saw them were they wearing bits of uniforms, were they looking shabby, were they -- the issues that you had, is that what they looked like? And that's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The basic thing is when you come into an area --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: -- occupied by a unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I just need to know yes or no: When you came across the 175th as a volunteer unit, were they in bits of random uniforms, were they looking shabby, were they not meeting the protocol that was set out by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And then there is a document 5D1359, which indicates the 252nd was inspected as well. Did you take part in any sort of inspection of the 252nd?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that I mentioned the 252nd in my report. I mentioned the 58th there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, it's -- the reason I'm asking the question is that was part of the series of documents that was listed by the Defence in regards to this witness, so I believe that he would have had something to say on them otherwise they would not have been listed, but it appears not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, you were discussing the 175th in the middle of April. There is in another document at 5D563 that is now dated the 19th of May, almost a full month after that, that's also indicating yet again, and this is after the time that you've removed those commanding officers, at number 4 that they're still being shown to have unauthorised leave, sloppy uniforms, theft continues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of precision, we did put the broader list in our notification, but when we were taking the statement from this witness we only used documents he was familiar with and we informed the Prosecution of this and said we would be using an abbreviated set of documents. I believe that the Prosecution received that notification from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, nothing's being made of it, Mr. Bakrac. Ms. Carter's moved on to something else, so let's concentrate on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, on 19 May 1999, another inspection is done that's indicating all of the concerns that were raised with the 175th back in April are still present after the removal of those officers. What was done to the unit after 19 May, given the fact that the circumstances had not changed, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the 19th of May, I can't remember whether I was there at all. I don't think I was, so I cannot comment on the situation in that unit. I was not able to be aware of every single inspection.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When in -- when units were being inspected, if members of the Pristina Corps came back and saw that the same issues were still present, what was the normal operating procedure in order to rectify that situation after the command has already been removed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: After touring and visiting the units, a report on the situation in the unit is submitted to the command, and it's up to the commander to decide whether there would be another inspection or whether certain measures should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And in this case you can't speak to what happened to the 175th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know what happened next. I know up to the point in time when the Chief of Staff and 15 officers were replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the inspection of the 354th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: 354th Brigade, I visited it, but I don't know why because that was a two-month period. It wasn't just one visit and one team. There may have been more than one team, and I may have visited that unit once or twice. If it's not a report I compiled, I cannot comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Tell me if based on your experience there is a Supreme Command Staff inspection report at 5D436 discussing the 354th. In it, it notes that there is a lack of training amongst these soldiers; they're being brought in but they're not being trained properly. Was that your experience when you were reviewing the 354th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information that soldiers from that unit were not well-dressed. What I saw met the appropriate criteria. I don't know on what matters the unit was inspected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I waited for the witness to finish answering, although I didn't wait for the interpretation to finish. But I think it would be fair to the witness when he's being asked a question to be shown the document on which the question is based so that we can all see what my learned friend is asking about and for the witness to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In view of his answer, you might regret that. But what do you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to show the witness 5D436 at page 3 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S noting paragraph 1 -- or number 1 in subsection 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would direct you to number 1 that indicates: "After the mobilisation a big part of the brigade did not undergo the necessary training and consolidation before being engaged." Are you telling me that as an officer inspecting this unit, you did not notice this but yet the Supreme Command Staff did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the -- I didn't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you ask that question again, please, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would direct you to number 1 that indicates: "After the mobilisation, a big part of the brigade did not undergo the necessary training and consolidation before being engaged." Are you telling me that as an officer inspecting this unit, you did not notice this but yet the Supreme Command Staff did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The assumption is that military conscripts or men liable for military service have done their military service, that they have gone through training, and on arrival in the units - and the corps commander insisted on this - that they should also be trained in war, perhaps at that point in time --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Clearly based on the Supreme Command Staff they didn't believe that that occurred. But now let's move on to subsection 5, it's the same page for you -- no, I'm sorry, it's page 4 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S at paragraph 5. There it indicates: "There are many bearded soldiers and officers in scruffy clothes and there is alcohol consumption. This is particularly characteristic of the 3rd." Will you please tell me, was that your experience with the 354th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I know about orders from the corps commander concerning the drinking of alcohol. He banned it --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: -- and they insisted on order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, why are you asking that sort of question? You get an answer: Yes, it doesn't add anything; you get the answer: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- it doesn't add anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, as we are dealing with a JCE 3 case, one of the concerns is the unit is acting up. If there are problems or issues within the unit, we have to determine whether reasonable efforts were made to rectify that situation. In this case it appears that the people who were actually inspecting these units and addressing these issues either were turning a blind eye to it and doing nothing, which is a problem; or they are seeing exactly what is happening and are misreporting up the chain. But in this case we see a superior unit is quite aware of it, but the people who can actually remove these people from position are doing nothing; so that's why I'm asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he's not in a position to remove them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the inspection teams, based on the inspection team's reports would go back to the Pristina Corps level, and that is the level at which they could actually be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- so let's assume that this witness does know -- or this is his experience, what difference does that make?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The difference would be what did they do about it. What did the Pristina Corps do if they saw all of this, what remedial measures did they take. In the 175th, they indicated they removed all commanders, but yet when coming back a month later did nothing when the same issues were taking place. In the 354th it appears we have a similar circumstance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but how does this witness assist you either way? It's the question I'm not following the purpose of.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- as he was a member of the inspection teams, and he would be the one advising superior command, his impressions of the unit or his lack of reporting on it would become relevant. However, if the Court is not assisted I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How would it add, though, if we've got here a clear statement of indiscipline, how does whether he agrees with it or disagrees with it improve the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Because the follow-up question would be at the end of what was done, if anything, to the 354th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I understand that, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So then I can jump through that to the last question then.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, it has been indicated by Supreme Command Staff that there are a number of issues between training, the lack of appearance, that briefing is not being done -- you indicated before that one of the things that needs to happen is that there has to be some sort of every-other-day inspection by the commander that appears not to be done. What, if anything, did the Pristina Corps do to rectify this problem?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that the corps commander constantly insisted, ordered, called upon the brigade commanders and the commanders of the independent battalions --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: -- to take all these measures --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I don't want to speak in hypotheticals. What I want to know is clearly a superior command has indicated major problems with the 354th. I want to know at the Pristina Corps level what was done in order to rectify these problems, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Certain command orders followed to solve these problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Marinkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Marinkovic, orders don't solve any problems, it's action. Ms. Carter's asking you what was actually done. We know what the orders say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what was specifically done in this unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: We'll move on to treatment of civilians. Do you have indication that -- or can you speak on the topic about how the civilian population was treated by the VJ units that were in the field?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The civilians were treated in the spirit of orders by the commander and respect for international humanitarian law --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Excuse me, any answer you're going to give is going to come back to you submitted orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I, no, nor do I have the right to issue orders nor was it my command duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The question becomes: Is your knowledge of what occurred in order to rectify any problems, is your knowledge going to be the Pristina Corps issued orders to follow humanitarian law and to do as they were told to do? Is that going to be the entirety of your answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Starting from 1998 all the way to the end of the war, orders were constantly issued some special --

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any experience what was done to implement these orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every order binds the commander to carry it out decisively to implement it. There is a deadline in every order and the commander has to be notified, he has to report back to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I ask quite simple questions, but obviously there is some sort of communication problem with you -- between you and me.
